title: Atomic-scale sensing of photoexcitation processes in electronically isolated molecules via atomic force microscopy
authors: Lisanne Sellies, Thomas Buchner, Jinhui Guo, Sonja Bleher, Felix Giselbrecht, Clea Ruth, Andrea Donarini, Jascha Repp, Laerte L. Patera
abstract: Atomic-scale insights into light-matter interaction can be obtained using light-assisted scanning probe microscopy techniques. Recently, photoexcited charge carriers have been detected by means of scanning tunnelling microscopy, enabling the study of photo-induced charge transfer with atomic-scale spatial resolution. Here, we propose an approach based on atomic force microscopy (AFM), namely photoexcitation single-charge AFM (PE-AFM), to detect photoexcitation in single molecules adsorbed on non-conductive dielectric films. Synchronizing laser pulses to the oscillation of the tip of an AFM enables the detection of electron tunnelling events that follow photoexcitation. We demonstrate the PE-AFM technique for individual copper phthalocyanine molecules and achieve photoexcitation-driven AFM contrast with ångström spatial resolution. The observed sub-molecular contrast suggests the involvement of a long-lived quadruplet excited state. When combined with the recently developed AFM excited-state spectroscopy including lifetime measurements, PE-AFM enables comprehensive characterization of electronic states involved in photoexcitation and subsequent intersystem crossing, establishing a powerful platform for investigating photophysical processes at the single-molecule level.
summary: The authors introduce Photoexcitation single-charge AFM (PE-AFM) to probe photoexcitation processes in isolated molecules. By synchronizing laser pulses with AFM tip oscillations, they detect charge transfer events related to excited states. This technique provides unprecedented atomic-scale characterization of molecular photophysics, revealing the role of long-lived electronic states.
main_problem: The primary goal is obtaining atomic-scale insights into photoexcitation processes and subsequent charge transfer dynamics within single, electronically isolated molecules.
main_result: The proposed Photoexcitation single-charge AFM (PE-AFM) technique successfully detects these photocurrents with angstrom spatial resolution, revealing the involvement of long-lived excited states like $	ext{Q}_1$.
method: The method combines Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) with synchronized nanosecond laser pulses to induce photoexcitation and measure subsequent electron tunneling events via changes in cantilever damping.
model_or_system: The system involves single molecules, such as copper phthalocyanine ($	ext{CuPc}$), adsorbed on non-conductive dielectric films ($	ext{NaCl}$) over a metal substrate. Theoretical modeling uses interacting Hamiltonians to describe the multi-state electronic structure (e.g., $	ext{D}_0$, $	ext{Q}_1$) and potential energy surfaces.
key_observables: Photoexcitation-driven AFM contrast, cantilever damping modulation ($\Delta f$), photoemission current, excited-state spectral features, and transition voltages ($V_G$).
important_parameters: Long-lived state lifetime ($	au \approx 11 \, \mu	ext{s}$), spatial resolution ($	ext{\AA}$), laser wavelength ($\lambda = 640 	ext{ nm}$), and gate voltage dependence.
main_assumptions: The technique assumes electronic decoupling of molecules via insulating films, and analysis often relies on modeling the rate-limiting step being dictated by the longest-lived excited state pathway.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate simulation results for near-field electric field enhancement in dielectric environments, the PE-AFM operating principle showing charge cycling, polarization dependence of the signal, and spatial maps revealing orbital selectivity based on gate voltage.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for atomic-scale photoexcitation sensing to detailing the PE-AFM methodology (including simulations), demonstrating its capability via spectroscopy and mapping ($	ext{CuPc}$), and finally using advanced fitting techniques to characterize long-lived excited state dynamics.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges quantum optics/molecular physics with nanoscale characterization. The ability to map out multi-state potential energy surfaces and measure lifetimes *in situ* at the single-molecule level is highly relevant for understanding open quantum systems dynamics in condensed matter.
